title: Take and read (Confessions 8.12)
hookLine: in the garden, a child's chant, Romans 13, and his long wavering ends
tomorrow: what did a mother and son touch at a window?

lines: THE SAME LINE, OVER AND OVER.
cards: Somewhere a kid is singing the same line over and over, the way kids do, until the whole house knows it by heart. A garden in Milan. Augustine has thrown himself down under a fig tree, crying.
How long, he says. Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now?
Why not this hour? Then, from a house nearby, a child's voice, a boy or a girl, he can't tell, chanting over and over: take up and read, take up and read.

teach.h: A CHILD'S CHANT, OVER AND OVER.
teach.b: Augustine stops crying and tries to think: do children sing those words in some game? He can't remember any. So he takes it as a command from God, to open the book and read the first passage he finds.
He remembers that Antony, from yesterday's story, once heard a Gospel read aloud and took it as spoken to him.

teach.h: THE FIRST LINES HIS EYES FALL ON.
teach.b: He hurries back to where Alypius is sitting, picks up the book of Paul's letters, and reads in silence the first lines his eyes fall on.

In the King James, from Romans: "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ."
He reads no further, he says. He doesn't need to. A light, like certainty, pours into his heart.
Then the small, human ending, the one to tell a friend.
Alypius asks to see it, and reads one line past where Augustine stopped: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye."
He takes that one for himself. Two friends, one book, and each finds his own verse.

how: Some Christians read scripture slowly and prayerfully, a practice often called lectio divina; churches and teachers differ on opening the Bible at random, and Augustine's garden comes up when they talk about it.

o: a chant that sent Augustine to read Romans
a teacher's order to study for an exam
a library rule for borrowing old books

games.q: take and read — tap the pairs.
p: where he threw himself down, crying
put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ

s: Augustine knew the chant from a children's game
he tried to remember one and couldn't. so he took it as a call.
Alypius read on and took the next verse for himself
him that is weak in the faith receive ye: Romans 14:1.
Augustine read the whole letter to the Romans that day
he read a few lines, he says, and no further; he didn't need to.

games.q: your little brother hears this story and decides to open the Bible at random before every test, to see if he'll pass. what fits Augustine's garden?
o: great plan: the first verse tells you what will happen.
Augustine read to be changed, not to get a forecast.
the Bible should never, ever be opened at random.
games.why: the chant sent him to read, and Romans spoke to how he would live. churches differ on opening at random, but it was never a forecast.

practice: Open a Bible, on paper or on a screen, to any page, and read the first few lines your eyes fall on, out loud and slowly. Listen to how they sound in the room.
Then sit with them for the rest of the time, without making them mean anything yet.

wordCard.voice: Take and read. A child's chant in a garden in Milan, a few lines of Romans, and the end of Augustine's long wavering.
